utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. We are here to hear a motion filed on the 14th of July, Defence motion for adjournment. The Chamber has carefully read that motion but would like to hear any additional submissions the parties would like to make, and since there is not a written response by the Prosecution, the Prosecution will have an opportunity to respond. And perhaps we first hear the Prosecution to hear what they've got to say about this motion and then hear further submissions by the Defence. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. My name is Mark Harmon. Appearing with me is Mr. Alan Tieger, Ms. Carmela Annink-Javier from the Office of the Prosecutor. We did not file a response, Your Honour. We felt that we could make any oral submissions after we heard the submissions of the Defence. Therefore, since it's not our motion, Your Honour, I would defer to the Defence to make its submissions and we would then reply if we deem replies are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had in mind, as a matter of fact, that you would respond to the written motion and the Defence would then have an opportunity to include that in its further submissions. So -- but if the parties could agree, like in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICC where the parties are supposed to agree on the order in court --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have absolutely no problem with Mr. Harmon's suggestion. That seems to be a side issue, really, that we can deal with everything effectively in the way that he suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then follow it. Mr. Stewart, you have an opportunity to make further submissions related to this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The -- Your Honour, what I -- there -- there -- we did put in quite a lot of factual detail in our motion and we outlined our legal submissions, but as Your Honour will appreciate, in the light of the enormous importance to Mr. Krajisnik and the Defence of this matter, there are quite a number of points that we would like to make clear. The -- what I'd like to do first, which may seem a little bit strange, but I'm going to run through several points to make it clear what this hearing isn't about. And it is important, Your Honour, because in order to understand clearly what this hearing is not about, that will focus on what it is about, and of course they are related. And it avoids any possible confusion of thinking or misunderstanding about the position of the Defence and the approach. So first of all, what this hearing is not about, is not about money. It's not about the financial allowance by the Registry in the sense that there is no application or complaint whatever -- Your Honour, I'm sorry, I should say I'm accompanied by my co-counsel Ms. Chrissa Loukas and our case manager Ms. Tatjana Cmeric. I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- for overlooking that. Whenever I say "I" I mean we anyway, Your Honour, because these are our submissions. It's -- there's no application, no complaint about that. Your Honour knows the basic system, of course is very familiar with it. Mr. Krajisnik is treated as partly indigent in this case so that there is a -- at this stage of the proceedings there is a gross monthly allowance -- that's a slight simplification, but there is a gross monthly allocation by the Registry for Defence costs to cover everything. Mr. Krajisnik has been assessed as liable to make a contribution to that, and, Your Honour, of course this Trial Chamber has dealt with that particular aspect of the matter and so is familiar with it and it's not appropriate or necessary for me to go into the details of the figures there, but that is the broad position as a matter of principle. This hearing is also nothing to do with any question about Mr. Krajisnik's contribution or any question of whether it's paid or not. That has not affected anything so far and the arrangements on which -- as a matter of fact, I am insisting as between myself and Mr. Krajisnik - which are absolutely not necessary to go into in the light of what I'm saying - mean that it shouldn't significantly affect the position in future either. So Your Honours can treat the matter on the footing that what the Defence team has had at its disposal and what it has at its disposal to manage this case and run this case with the people that we have in The Hague and the people that we have out in -- well, it's mainly in Pale, Bosnia Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, that we are managing that with the amount which is allocated to us by the Registry, which is a standard amount for a category 3, the most difficult and leadership case. If the Trial Chamber has any concerns about that basic point as I've put it, then, as I will under a number of other points, I invite the Trial Chamber to express any such doubts and questions so I can answer them, because there is an answer to that. We clearly don't -- we want to avoid any misunderstanding and we don't want to hear in a judgement at any point some misunderstanding which we believe we could have cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I could give you an answer to that right away. Of course we -- it will not surprise you that the Chamber has already exchanged some views on -- on this motion, and it was clearly understood and it's the starting point for the Chamber that it will not interfere with how and whether or not Mr. Krajisnik fulfils his obligations to contribute. The Chamber just takes it for granted that a full Defence team is functioning. The size of the team, of course, has been mentioned, but it's not something the Chamber is concerned about at this moment as to whether you can function on the basis of the decision of the Registrar as it stands after review by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, with respect, there is a slightly different point. The question of how we are able to function on that allowance is a question, and it is relevant to what we have. The -- the point is a very slightly different one but I think it's probably wrapped up in what Your Honour was saying anyway, which is that the Trial Chamber can take it that there is no difference from the practical point of view of this application, this hearing. There's no difference between the situation as it would be if Mr. Krajisnik had been assessed at a nil contribution and we were getting the whole amount from the Registry and the situation where we're not. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what, perhaps not very precisely, I wanted to express.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand. That's extremely helpful, Your Honour, because that clears that point out of the way straight away. The second matter it's not about is the project, as I will call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The third already. The first was the money, the second was the contribution and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The contribution is very much part of the money. I've got my own numbering system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will not interfere any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour, that was all part of number one. So I'm moving on to number 2. What -- the second thing this hearing is not about is the project, as we called it, and its end last Monday. And perhaps in about two or three sentences, Your Honour, I should recap what the project was because it's a public hearing. It's now aborted, in a sense. Whether it's dead or it's comatose or it's sleeping depends on point of view and where we might go in future. But Your Honour knows that what we did was that we -- well, I hope Your Honour accepts that we conscientiously, Prosecution and Defence, explored agreement on facts, particularly in relation to municipalities and, although we hadn't got very far on experts, the question of agreement of expert evidence, consistently with our duties to Mr. Krajisnik on our side and the Tribunal on both sides, but in -- on -- and what we had, as Your Honours know, we had a programme or a schedule which might have run quite a number of weeks into the future and after the recess during which we would attempt to agree facts in relation to a whole series of municipalities in the interests of, in the end, trying to avoid unnecessary disputes and trying to, in everybody's interests, move this trial on, consistently, of course, with Mr. Krajisnik's interests and our duties to the Tribunal. In a nutshell, Your Honour knows, of course, our duties to the Tribunal don't positively require the Defence to agree facts where it's not in Mr. Krajisnik's interests, because it's accepted as a basic principle that the defendant has a right that the Prosecution proves every single ingredient in their case. It may be not a productive approach to adopt in a case overall, but it is a defendant's right. And Your Honour I'm far from saying that we are intending to exercise that right to the full in those terms. That's -- we don't see that as being our professional position and necessary in Mr. Krajisnik's interests, but as far as the particular project is concerned, Your Honour knows, because I wrote, having decided over the weekend that it was no longer in Mr. Krajisnik's interests, that was my professional judgement, shared by our team, that it was correct to inform the Tribunal immediately and notify the Trial Chamber immediately so that there was no room for further misunderstanding and no unnecessary work by anybody. The -- we -- so that's -- well, I think, actually, I can move on from number 2, because number 3 - and I make this a separate point because it's related to the project but it is important - is again what this hearing is not about is the project timetable. We spent, as Your Honour knows, a few weeks ago we all - by which I mean many members of the Prosecution team and for practical purposes all members of the Defence core team; myself, Ms. Loukas and Ms. Cmeric - spent, for practical purposes, a week planning the project, producing a schedule. That was quite a heavy exercise in itself. We also spent, for practical purposes, pretty much the whole of the last two weeks, not including this current week but the previous two weeks, almost entirely on that work because we were implementing the project at that stage. So those two weeks, for practical purposes, disappeared on that exercise. The idea of the extended adjournment, or one of the important ideas of the extended adjournment, and certainly from the Defence point of view, was that it would enable us to have a certain amount of time to catch up on the preparation of this case which we have so far not been able anywhere near to complete, which is the basis of this application. So even if one were to take the project timetable as the guide, we would need the time contemplated in the schedule, because we've already had -- and a lot of this week has gone by as well and not been available because of this motion for proper preparation on the case. So we are effectively three weeks on from when even that schedule had to begin. But I do emphasise the point that the schedule inherent in that project was a negotiated time. It was a compromise. We did, on the Defence side, and we put it frankly, we did wish to avoid the risks of this sort of application because, after all, we hope and trust in the end that our application will be granted, but it would be naive of me to stand here and say that I don't know, as an experienced advocate, that there are risks inherent in this application. That's not in any way to suggest that it doesn't have absolute strength, shouldn't be granted, but we know there are risks; otherwise, the Trial Chamber would just be saying, fine, you can have what you want and the Prosecution would be saying that's fine, we go along with that. We know that's not the position. Here we are having to fight it very hard. So that was a negotiated compromise which, in our view, in the end, with all the other elements, and Your Honour knows from the meeting last Friday it's our position we don't suggest that the Trial Chamber agree with us at the moment and we don't know whether the trial -- the Prosecution agree with us or not, really, showed insufficient concern for Mr. Krajisnik's interests, but we hope that the project at least has the merit of enabling the Tribunal to see some of the whole picture. The test now is what's needed to ensure a fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik from now, from this moment. And if the Trial Chamber draws the inference that because we would have compromised in all sorts of ways on a particular period and on the footing of clear assurances on which we could rely as to the time we would have, that that's all we reasonably need, then that's a wrong inference because that is not the position. We accept the obligation this afternoon to flesh out that point and to indicate very clearly, in a way that perhaps we have not sufficiently done before, and perhaps the opportunity, circumstances haven't arisen because we haven't had a motion in this form. It's our obligation, of course, to give the Tribunal -- to give the Trial Chamber the clear facts, because we are asking - we acknowledge that - we are asking for a very significant adjournment in a very heavy case, but we accept that obligation and we will do that. The fourth point that this hearing isn't about, except in a very -- in an indirect way, it's not about the time or money spent by or on the previous Defence team. The time and money spent, and just again to recap, we're in a public hearing: Mr. Krajisnik has been in prison here in The Hague since April 2000. His trial, with a team of lead and co-counsel, the lead counsel being Mr. Brashich, was due to start -- I can never remember the precise date. It was either the 12th or 17th of May, but it was some date in the middle of May 2003. And as Your Honours know all too well, a matter of a few weeks before that trial Mr. Brashich had to be or was removed from the case because he basically lost his qualification because he was suspended from practice by the New York Bar. Whether it's city or state, again I don't know, but his Bar. He was suspended from practice from the 1st of May, 2003, and normally speaking, and certainly that was the position adopted in relation to Mr. Brashich, a lawyer who loses his standing for a period or permanently in his or her own jurisdiction is, by the same token, going to lose his or her standing and right to appear in front of this Tribunal unless a special dispensation is offered, and it wasn't. Mr. Brashich's co-counsel was apparently also not ready and equipped or, in effect, expecting ever to have to step into the position of actually having to do the case as an advocate, so he had to go as well. Whether had to go or did go, it's -- I leave that entirely open, I can't remember which it was, and I don't mean any -- he certainty wasn't in the same position as Mr. Brashich. I don't wish to suggest or imply that so far as the reasons for removal of his own. Basically, he went with Mr. Brashich. That's what happened. There was then a period of a few months over the summer until I was assigned as lead counsel on 31st of July, 2003, and then Ms. Loukas signed as co-counsel on a date which she may remember but I don't -- 16th of September, 2003. Thank you. The reason why I say the time and money spent by the previous team are completely irrelevant, they're completely irrelevant except so far as they affect the time, and I can put in brackets money but it's really the time, the time required by the present team. So it's actually only such time saving as the present team is able to, if you like, have achieved or such time saving as transferred over to us when we took over the case by virtue of the fact that work had already been done by the previous Defence team which is of any relevance at all. Now, there was some, of course, because there were some preliminary motions. There were some steps along the way, some procedural steps which any Defence team would have to be engaged in, which Mr. Brashich and his co-counsel were engaged in. There was some water under the bridge. There were some steps which simply didn't have to be repeated. Those were relatively -- relatively minor in the overall context of preparation of the case. The previous Defence team did also file a Defence pre-trial brief. They have saved us time, it's true, in the sense that we have not been required -- we were given the opportunity of supplementing the pre-trial brief, but frankly, we were not in the business of volunteering any tasks that we didn't absolutely have to undertake at that stage. So although the pre-trial brief might be thought to be rather less informative than pre-trial briefs sometimes are, and that's a bit of an understatement, it is true that we have not actually had to prepare a pre-trial brief. So we have never suggested that there was no saving whatever, that we are in exactly the same position as a new team taking over from scratch with nothing. But that still raises the question of how far we really have been saved the requirements of normal preparation time by the work done by the previous Defence team. And the simple answer is not very far. Now, one of the problems here is that, in a way, the people in the best position to judge, if I might usurp that word but not intending to usurp Your Honours' functions -- perhaps assess is a better word. The people best able to assess whether that really has been a savings is us, actually, the Defence team, because we know because we see because we got the results of that work --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm asked to slow down, which I will try to remember to do. The -- so however unsatisfactory the Krajisnik case past and present expenditure might look, and we know and they're quite notorious some aspects of the financial expenditure on this case up to Easter last year, but however unsatisfactory the expenditure might look and the budget might look, and we're quite sure they do, we can imagine perfectly well there's been plenty of anxious discussion about the expenditure on the Krajisnik case here and in New York, and anywhere else for that matter that has an interest in the matter, but none of that money can properly be retrieved by cutting corners on what's needed from this moment on for the presentation of Mr. Krajisnik's defence. We are very sorry to say but it is a fact that that money is just lost. It's bygones. If it is regarded by those in control of the money as wasted, then again we are very sorry. I don't mean we lose sleep over it, Your Honour, because, frankly, we have other things to do, but it is unfortunate, of course. Any wasted money at that level is unfortunate, very unfortunate. But it is not Mr. Krajisnik's responsibility, it is not for Mr. Krajisnik to pay for it directly, indirectly. It is not for any part of this institution and certainly not for this Trial Chamber with the heavy responsibility to attempt any retrieval of that money or any compensation for that money or time lost by cutting corners on what is needed. That is absolutely fundamentally wrong in principle. The fifth point that this hearing is not about -- and I've nearly got to the end of the points it's not about, Your Honour, because I'm quite sure the Trial Chamber would like me to move on to what it is, that seems a reasonable request. The fifth point it's not about is it's not about Mr. Krajisnik's right to expedition of his trial. I've given the basic timetable. The removal of Mr. Krajisnik's previous team from his defence wasn't his fault. The circumstances of Mr. Brashich's suspension by the New York Bar were absolutely unrelated to anything to do with this Tribunal, as far as one could see anyway. It certainly wasn't Mr. Krajisnik's fault. He has never had any incentive to delay his case a day longer than needed for it to be properly prepared and presented. He is adamant he's not guilty. Of course he pleads not guilty, but he doesn't seek and hasn't sought to seek to delay -- he hasn't sought to delay or defer the trial. And certainly, Your Honour, we can assure you we have seen not a single thing to suggest that since we took over. It is his right -- I might put it this way; it sounds a bit, well, tendentious. A lot of things are tendentious, but in a way, it's his right to have the trial slowed down rather than expedited. It is his right to have the trial slowed down slower than perhaps others with a different perspective might think was a good thing so far as necessary to enable his Defence team and him to conduct his defence properly. So it sounds an odd way of putting it but that's certainly his right. It's his right to have the trial proceed no faster than is consistent with his being able properly to present his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one of the issues the Chamber, Mr. Stewart, has already exchanged views on. The right of Mr. Krajisnik to an expeditious trial will not be used against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obliged. Thank you. I can move straight on. What this hearing isn't about as well is -- well, it either is or it isn't in a way. It's certainly not about hard work. It is about hard work in the fundamental sense; it's hard work for everybody involved. But it's certainly not about hard work in the sense that I believe that -- and I express a personal belief here, I don't believe anybody is suggesting or ever has suggested that Mr. Krajisnik's Defence team doesn't work enormously hard. Certainly as far as every other member of my team is concerned, apart from where I stand, that's undoubtedly true. So we take it as accepted as a given some of my team work superhumanly hard. So with that, I can move on to what this hearing is about. Well, obviously it's about adequate time to prepare. That's apparent. That's in the motion. It's about, in a sense, if I acknowledge that there is a balance of resources and time, that isn't to suggest or to resile from the basic point that we must have whatever time is necessary to present Mr. Krajisnik's defence properly, and there is no balance or there is no equation to be achieved between the budget for this case and that. There is no trade-off that is permissible there if a particular step or a particular timetable or a particular schedule carries any significant risk in relation to the fair presentation of Mr. Krajisnik's defence. Then, and we put it very starkly in order to highlight the principle in our motion, there is a stark choice there. Either the trial does not proceed in that way and an adjustment is made to allow Mr. Krajisnik to present his defence fairly, or the charges have to be dropped and he must be released. There is no middle way. This is not possible for a Trial Chamber for this Tribunal, it is not possible for any trial to be conducted, whatever the cost, in a way which does not allow the defendant the adequate opportunity of presenting his defence. We have summarised in our motion what we regard as the key points in relation to this aspect of the matter, and Your Honour finds those, I hope conveniently, summarised in paragraph 10 of the written motion. And then in each case we have expanded them a little bit in two or three paragraphs usually. We've given a summary of what we say are the key points under those chapter headings, if you like. And some of the points, some more closely than others, some of the points tie in with the relatively detailed chronology which we have annexed to the motion which essentially describes what's happened in relation to the conduct of the defence case, in relation to materials, broadly in relation to the nature of the involvement of the particular people, right through to date since I first came into the case at the very end of July 2003, right through up until we wrote -- well, until we filed this motion this week. The -- the wide range of issues, as we say in the motion, this is well understood by the Chamber but we thought it helpful given the nature of the hearing and Your Honours' expressed concerns that the public should understand what is going on. We felt it helpful to summarise, and perhaps summarising a case of this size in about three paragraphs is itself a task, but we hope we've done that accurately. It's -- again, we take it as a given the Trial Chamber knows what the issues are. The Trial Chamber knows what the wide-ranging and complex nature of the issues in this case, involving as they do very detailed evidence often about local events but the thrust of the case being to link them to the central leadership of the SDS and particularly, of course, to link them to this defendant, Mr. Krajisnik. And it's summarised, and I don't think I need go through the summary there. It's available publicly anyway what we set out. Some of what we say in the motion we still think it's useful background to put in but, of course, it's obvious. Of course to present Mr. Krajisnik's defence requires a sound knowledge and understanding of the historical and political context. That's, in a sense, it's a statement of the obvious, but it ties in with this, Your Honour: Some of these issues overlap. The -- when Ms. Loukas and I came into the case, broadly at the same time because although assigned in September Ms. Loukas came here in August with a view to being assigned to the case and we did spend a few days when Mr. Brashich was also in The Hague, so I don't suggest Ms. Loukas came into the case cold in the middle of September, because she did, of course, begin to get involved in August. We came into the matter like many but not all Defence counsel in this case, of course, with at least we would like to think that we had as much knowledge of the events in former Yugoslavia and in the early 1990s as what we like to think we are, which is educated layman as far as that is concerned. We don't claim any more. We would be reluctant to admit to any less but perhaps others can judge that. But I do suggest that nobody should overestimate what that actually involves. I can give Your Honours a very simple example. And Your Honour has been a Defence counsel in this Tribunal and knows, for example, the sometimes troublesome matter of invoices and what you can get paid for and so on. We've had a query raised. We have had -- we're not making a big issue of this with the Registry about this, it's just an illustration. We have had a charge for time either rejected or queried, I forget which but I think it was rejected, on the basis that time spent finding out about the setting up of Republika Srpska and the way it was constituted, we can't charge for that because we're supposed to know it. Well, I asked four or five people where I work in London if they'd ever heard of it, and I don't mean any offence to Mr. Krajisnik but not one of them had ever heard of it or had any idea what it was. And my colleagues are at least averagely well-educated, I will say that in their favour. It's a bit unreal, that. We don't come with that sort of knowledge. But the point is not to have a moan about charging. We could be here for weeks if we do that. The point is to indicate that there's a huge amount of -- it is in fact non-chargeable, as it happens, but there is a huge amount of background work to be done by anybody coming, as we did, straight into a case like this. And we also came into it, may we respectfully remind the Court, we came into it in circumstances where there wasn't a lead-in to it. There wasn't a negotiation and understanding that we come into the case and then in two or three months time it would start to get going and we'd be at phase 1 and so on and then there would be the preliminary motions and so on. We came into it pretty much like that in the late summer of 2003. Now, I confess there was only so much I could do in August because - surprise, surprise - I have four children, as it happens, we needn't go into the details, but everybody has commitments in the summer. Everybody has things -- they really can't just drop everything and get started and work every day on this case but not going into all those personal things, that would be inappropriate. But it's just an obvious point. Actually I'm also, apart from that, I'm a practising barrister. That's what I do, and so I do, if I'm lucky, have clients. I do -- I do have a job. I am in London. Ms. Loukas had a job in Sydney at the time, which she has actually given up to come and do this case full time. But she couldn't do that immediately, she had a couple of months to get out of her job. She had awhile to come out of Australia. Actually, as it happens, she came here to The Hague full time much earlier than is deemed necessary by this institution, and "deemed" in the sense of deemed and ready to pay for it. The official position of this institution so far has been that co-counsel can turn up a week before the trial. That, of course, is so absurd that we took upon ourselves the considerable amount of the responsibility and expense of ensuring that it wasn't left until that point and we provided that degree of those extra facilities and that extra work, so that, as it happens, Ms. Loukas arrived in November, November the 15th, just before the financial hearing that Your Honour may remember. She wasn't so directly involved in that but she happened to arrive around that time. And she's been here, for practical purposes, with a few odd days here and there where she can twist my arm, somewhere else, but pretty much here all the time. I haven't in the same way because, after all, I live in London and I work in London so it's not quite the same problem, although -- well Your Honours have seen me here quite a lot. I am, for practical purposes, here now and I've hardly been to London recently very much except for a few hours here and there at a time. So the -- the -- what I'm coming to Your Honour, is the first two, three months -- and we can produce detailed figures but we don't believe that the point necessarily requires or lends itself to some tremendous elaborate statistical analysis -- the first few months we were not anyway able simply to -- sorry, Your Honour, for that gesture. We were not able to -- get the sound effects as well, probably. But we were not able to switch just immediately to full-time work on this case. There had to be a run-in. By the time we got to the end of the year, and really it took about that long, by the time we got to the end of the year, yes, we were. Certainly Ms. Loukas, when she was here was able to. I did have more difficulty, frankly, and I've indicated -- I should say on the chronology, memory plays tricks. Although the broad thrust of what I say about March is true, I'd actually misremembered the balance, as Your Honour may see. There's a reference to other commitments I had and time I spent. On checking, it turns out that actually the balance was slightly different and I spent more time in The Hague in the first half of the month, less time in the second half of the month but, Your Honour, I assure you the thrust of what we're saying is broadly correct there, it's just that I've misremembered the details of it. But the fact is, Your Honour, there was no -- there was no escaping that obligation on which -- as a matter of fact, the other clients were incredibly patient because I had to defer a whole lot of work there for two months to accommodate the start date of this trial on the 3rd of February. There's no need to go into detail about that, Your Honour, and of course I can't and shouldn't in relation to that other matter anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if you allow me to ask you one question in this respect. You were talking about the month of March whereas on the 23rd of April during a hearing where time was also an issue discussed, you then said that you were not able to work, as you said it, on this case from Wednesday morning through Sunday evening. You even said that you were perfectly happy to explain the reasons, they were essentially a combination of professional and personal. That's something different from what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which date was that, Your Honour? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 23rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it -- it -- it would have been an entirely different matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether it's the same as you're referring to in the annex to the motion as early March and what you now say might well have been the second part of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on reflection, I can't say that for sure. What I can say is that the matter that I was dealt -- that I dealt with in March was very largely concluded and dealt with by the time it got to the end of April but there was a bit residual work but I doubt -- all I can say, Your Honour, I doubt whether that would have demanded very much of my time but the combination of -- the combination of professional and personal, as I described it, I frankly can't remember what it was, Your Honour, but from time to time, especially with being here all the time and things getting deferred, from time to time there are things personal that just have to be dealt with. So I -- I can't remember what it was, Your Honour. To be frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether it was the same or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- but it was a sort of residual sorting out of the final bits and pieces in relation to that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The -- and that matter has totally gone and was totally gone a month or two ago now, which is just as well, but it was very demanding. It was, as I made clear, it was a pre-existing commitment when I -- when I took on this particular trial but I didn't know the scale of timing of that commitment because it's as unpredictable as many matters are. I'm not apologetic about it, Your Honour, I just -- I just give it to the Tribunal frankly, as I should do, as -- in the professional spirit of open disclosure in relation to such matters. That's my job, to be -- to be frank with the Trial Chamber. It's part of my job. My job's also to defend Mr. Krajisnik, of course. The -- so -- so far as the -- well, the range of issues -- I don't think I need elaborate that. The circumstances in which Ms. Loukas and I came to the case, we inherited Ms. Cmeric. I'm extremely glad we did, as it happens. She chose herself but we would certainly have chosen her, had we known, and we do. So we inherited Ms. Cmeric who had, in fact, been involved in this case, well, most of the time though there was a period of about three or four months when she'd actually resigned and was then coaxed back but she hasn't done that to us yet. So -- so Ms. Cmeric actually joined us in the sense of joining our team early on, though she was not able to come to The Hague except for odd days. She was specifically involved in the financial hearing and she was paid for by the Registry to come here, but there's no question of them paying for her to come here in the pre-trial period until immediately before the trial. And these are -- it is not easy to prepare for a case of this size on the footing that your team are not even allowed to constitute themselves in the same place at the same time with the case materials. And that's simply a fact. It's not -- it doesn't matter whether it's right, wrong, what the complaints are, you know, what -- what beefs we have about the money, it is simply a fact as far as the ability to prepare for this case is concerned, which is what's important for present purposes. The -- so far as the case materials are concerned, we have set out in some detail the -- as part of the hand-over from the previous team, the difficulties that we had in relation to previous case materials. We got previous case materials -- case materials which have been in the hands of the previous team. It's -- in a way, it's hard to -- it's hard to get across the complete shambles in which that material was. We describe it in black and white. It was an absolute mess. The stuff we got from Mr. Kostich was just packed up in boxes, many of which had never been opened. They'd come from somewhere else, and we couldn't tell from the outside what they were anyway. We couldn't tell on the inside sometimes what they were at the stage we looked at them. It was a complete mess. We have indicated Mr. Brashich's material -- we have to say this bluntly, and frankly we -- it's not proper for us to say anything which is not true. It's not part our brief to attack Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich, but it is part of our Defence of Mr. Krajisnik to say absolutely frankly what we found and what we received. We have -- we must say we have the strongest suspicion, and we voiced this, that the time during which we did not receive the material from Mr. Brashich, who was supposed to bring it with him when he came in August, a week was arranged for him to come in the first half of August, I believe, around the 11th, 12th, something like that -- I just confirm that is about roughly right -- he was supposed to bring the case materials with him because he had been ordered by the Registry originally and then again ordered to hand over the materials, but he didn't. He brought a few bits and pieces of paper here and there, but we didn't get that stuff and we didn't get it for about another six or seven weeks from Mr. Brashich, and we have the strongest suspicion that those six and seven weeks were used to give some semblance of order to the material and he simply wasn't in a position to hand it over. We'll never know that but that's the way it looked to us. But we got that material. I had dozens, I think it was, it felt like dozens and it certainly was more than just two or three or four, it was seven, eight, nine, ten, it was something like that, constant stream of emails and fax communication with Mr. Brashich to try to get the material out of Mr. Kostich, which we were told for a long time was about the same order in terms of volume as Mr. Brashich had got. That turned out not to be true. It was about two or three times as much probably in sheer quantity of paper, though what it amounted to is perhaps another matter. We have -- I went down to our office this morning, Your Honour, where we have had, as we indicate, teams of interns and assistants working. We now have quite a large team. We've actually got a list of our team, but just recently because it's that time of year as well. We've got an influx of extra help. We actually have -- I must say, looking at their CVs, we have a team I'll be amazed if a couple of them aren't Judges in international tribunals in years to come, but certainly at the moment they're young people with legal -- law degrees and so on. We have two B/C/S speakers now as legal assistants, which is a great help to us, because may I also remind the Trial Chamber that an advantage which Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich had which we don't have is they both spoke Serbian. They -- they are Serbs, in fact, and US citizens but Mr. Brashich's born in Belgrade. They didn't have any difficulty with Serbian. They didn't need to have documents translated. So we -- we got the stuff, and we can't complain about that because that's the position they were in when they were working on the case, so no complaint about that. But of course the material that came from Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich was a mixture of English and material in Serbian. Plenty was in English and plenty have been translated, and of course all the court documents are in English. We're not suggesting -- I don't want to exaggerate it, but there is lots and lots, and I mean lots and lots and lots of material which is not in English. And we have had one of the two young people that we've had working sorting out for months now in the way that we described does read easily. He -- he also is of a family from that part of the world. In fact, he's a Dutch citizen and lives here and studies here but he works for us part time. We have had that. We now have another young man who -- he is a Swedish citizen, but again he speaks absolutely -- and Ms. Cmeric confirms that his Serbian is as good as hers. He has no trouble at all with that. So we do have people and have had people for a long time who are able to do that sifting. But we haven't even finished the job yet because we -- we can't do it as far as the Serbian stuff is concerned but there are limits, and I know from observations that Your Honour has made in the past that Your Honour wouldn't expect and would be slightly dismayed if he and Your Honour's colleagues felt that Ms. Loukas and I had spent large numbers of hours sifting through boxes down at the office because that isn't really what we should be doing. That wouldn't be good management of the case. This task has not even been finished. I went down there this morning, obviously deliberately with a view to -- it's not the first time I've been there this week, I don't mean that. I've been down there quite a bit. But I went down there this morning to do a random sample just to give Your Honours an indication, and it was completely random, and the first pile of papers that I picked up not yet sorted, I opened it like a pack of cards and I came across a report of the Secretary-General from the Security Council, or Security Council report 11th of November, 1992, relating to the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. That's what Mr. Okun was giving evidence about. Now, that material is available in the world, but we -- we couldn't go -- realistically go foraging around in the world to find all those reports. We didn't have the time and the facilities and the opportunity to do that before we cross-examined Mr. Okun. It's a pity that when we got stuff like that -- I haven't read it this morning, Your Honour, I've had a look at it -- it's a pity that when we have stuff like that actually in our physical possession but have not time to know that we've got it in our physical possession that we ended up having to cross-examine Mr. Okun without reading that material. And I've indicated to Your Honour that this problem of unread material is enormous, and we do rather suggest that we doubt that the Prosecution have large quantities of material in their possession which no member of the Prosecution team has read. We would be surprised if equality of arms in this case had led to the position where both sides had very substantial quantities of absolutely unread material. And that's a very serious problem for us. The second item I picked out at random from a different pile was minutes of the War Presidency of the county, it was called in translation, the opstina at Celinac, 23rd of July, 1992. Now, I can't say that's not somewhere else in the papers. I can't at this second recall. It might be there as one of the documents in Mr. Treanor's material. It might easily be. But I'm just saying what I found. I found a draft translation of a statement from somebody I'm not able to identify from the contents relating to Bosanski Brod. Not a municipality we've got to yet, as it happens, as luck would have it, but there's no reason to suppose there's not similar material lurking in those papers relating to some municipalities we have already dealt with. I found a duplicate of set of statements. That was fine. We've got 70 per cent of the way to having a complete and well organised file of all the material relating to all the witnesses on the Prosecution list. I found some surrogate sheets, videos. Those don't really amount to a row of beans. That's the surrogate sheets don't amount to a row of beans, really. An interview with Mr. Karadzic from an organisation called Rights and Wrongs, The Global Centre, in May 1993. I found -- I found some articles which might or might not be helpful. I found a many page summary of a documentation database from an international human rights law institute. It would be quite nice to actually look through there and see what is of interest there, but they're not direct case materials. And then I -- a big stack of stuff in Serbian - and I call it Serbian because I think it is Serbian in this case, Your Honour - which our assistant Mr. Jonovic went through with me. It contains some extremely strange items, such as an advertisement for something to do with the upbringing of snakes, which doesn't seem very directly related to the case but the problem is we're not actually able to know that without reading it. We have no idea what it is. It's extraordinary stuff. But there are some journals. There's some material relating to somebody who worked for the -- or was paid out of the public funds of Republika Srpska. As far as this morning's exercise, impossible for me to know what all this stuff is about, but certainly the stuff to do with snakes was a bit weird. Something to do with export-export, something called Uniset Export-Import Banja Luka. Neither Mr. Jonovic nor I were able, in most cases, to have the faintest idea what it was really about, just on a cursory reading, because I was only asking him just what is it? What's the nature of it? One seems to be a poem and then it's to do with snakes, and then -- but then more official looking documents. There's all sorts of, maybe it's drafts, maybe it's significant; I simply don't know is the answer. But the scale of this problem is very large for us. We -- I -- there are enough problems for us with simply that material. The additional matters we've indicated, this -- the question of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We said, and Your Honour knows, that we -- we've not spent nearly as much, nearly as much time out there as we would have liked to. I cancelled the planned trip in March. I caught up with it up to a point in May. I had to chop that shorter than I wanted to because I simply didn't feel safe about spending that much time away from here. I haven't -- as I indicated, I have had no opportunity -- I haven't been round Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republika Srpska. I haven't had a chance to look at any of these municipalities. I don't mean I've never set foot in them. I've been to Banja Luka. I've been to Doboj. I've been through Zvornik. I've driven through no doubt a few other places, but that's all. I've had meetings in some of those places. I haven't -- I've seen some of the relevant locations and places in Sarajevo and Pale. I have seen those because they're -- they're pretty close by and Pale is where we go and that's where our office is. I have seen those; I've seen the parliament building and where the deputy's club was. I've seen those. That's about it. And I had never been. I'd been to that part of the world before. I'd never been to Bosnia and Herzegovina before in my life until I became involved in this case. Ms. Loukas has been once, just for about two days. There is an enormous quantity of material in the office in Pale. It's -- the question of management of the team in Pale and the question of management of their work is a serious one. There is -- in a sense there's a -- there's a difficulty that -- of course, Mr. Krajisnik takes on some of that management. I'll be absolutely blunt: Mr. Krajisnik is here. He and I don't always see eye-to-eye about the management of such matters. Because I am lead counsel in this case, Mr. Krajisnik, though is the person who faces these very serious charges, and it's pretty obvious the sort of issues that that might give rise to. The problem is there isn't time to resolve these issues. That's the difficulty. There isn't time and there hasn't been time to instruct them properly and control them properly, frankly, to sift the material. If we ask for a report from them, there's not properly time to go through it. We have simply been, since the beginning of this case, even with the breaks that we've had -- and we know and we understand, Your Honour, that that was a -- that was a valiant attempt by all concerned to make up for the fact that we did have to start this trial on the 3rd of February when we were really not ready. And that was, I believe, fully accepted that at that point this trial could not genuinely start as a functioning trial for the longer term on the 3rd of February. Whatever the reasons for starting it then, that was the position. There has been -- we appreciated that the Tribunal offered flexibility in relation to those first few weeks and there was then a valiant attempt by all concerned to enable us to catch up on it. Unfortunately, that attempt has failed. Whatever the reasons, it has failed. The -- that period -- and I've been frank about difficulties I faced in catching up with other matters during that period. I'm absolutely open about that, as I will be about everything else, Your Honour. But as far as the team who were in The Hague all the time during that period was concerned - I was here quite a lot of time, after all, as well - they were absolutely swamped; 92 bis stuff and just went on from one week to the next. There was never the opportunity to stand back. There was never the opportunity to sort the matter out. And we have constant To Do lists. Everybody has To Do lists but we have lists of To Do lists. And we haven't done them. We've done some of them. And Mr. Krajisnik is, quite fairly, always saying what about all these items on the To Do list? And I'm having to say I can't do them because I've got another To Do list and I've got to try and do that To Do list before I do the other To Do list. Now, much litigation and many cases are like that because it's a very demanding, heavy business, and any team and any lawyers are used to something which not in every other job, there are other hard jobs in the world, of course there are, but in many other jobs in many other areas of activity that would be -- people wouldn't want to live a life like that and they wouldn't want to do it, but in some masochistic way we like doing it and this is what we do for a job. But there are limits and we have gone well beyond them in this case because what we don't like -- and if we may put it that way, Your Honour, we accept the obligation to work very hard. We accept that there are pressures. We accept that sometimes one has to take a robust view on what can and can't be done. What we feel very uncomfortable and very unhappy about accepting is when we have to put what would normally be regarded as essential tasks and essential work on the case on one side because we just can't do it. And when we are prioritising between six essential tasks and we can only do two of them, we come to the conclusion that we are not able to defend Mr. Krajisnik properly, and he knows it and we know it, and it is a hard task and we found it a hard task. We hope that in the end it will be a successful task, to explain and give this Trial Chamber more information, as we are trying to do today, so that Your Honours have the advantage, which we haven't been able to give you before, of really understanding what is the problem here. And we must always remind ourselves, with respect, of the utmost gravity of the charges faced by Mr. Krajisnik. These are -- we don't feel that this is capable of much contradiction -- they are really the gravest criminal charges it is possible for a person to face. Genocide. There isn't a more serious charge. And that's what Mr. Krajisnik faces. And a whole lot of other charges as well. And we don't even need to enter into what the sentence might be for Mr. Krajisnik if he's convicted on all these charges, because it doesn't really need much thought to know that it's -- it's not going to be a light sentence. So that Mr. Krajisnik, as a 59-year-old man - I believe he's 59 - faces the most serious charges possible, and whatever the history of this matter, corners simply cannot be cut. We have never invited -- well, perhaps we have, I don't know. If we have invited Your Honours to accept simply as a professional assertion by us that we haven't been and aren't in a position to defend Mr. Krajisnik properly, perhaps we have put it that way, and it's not improper for us to put it that way, but we do understand that the Trial Chamber has the responsibility to be sure that it knows enough about what the position is to make a judgement, and that's what we're trying to do this afternoon. We're entirely open to any questions on the matter, apart from those matters which are obviously privileged and obviously we must keep them to ourselves and we can't be expected to answer, we have not the slightest compunction in dealing with any question and being entirely open about anything that we are doing in any aspect of the preparation of this case. We have absolutely nothing to hide, because the more the circumstances of this matter are exposed and the more it becomes clear what it is we're faced with, what we've had to do and what we have to do, the more obvious it is that we cannot defend Mr. Krajisnik at the moment without this adjournment that we seek, and then there is the question then of how we proceed, because we are a small team. And the point we made, we like to think we make up in quality, but others can judge that, but what we must have, the only way, as we say in the motion, the Prosecution have a larger team. They do. We don't blame them for that. We're not requiring them to jettison two or three of their people because we feel it's a bit hard that they've got more people than us. I mean, they're very nice people, but we don't ask them to do that. But what it does mean is that because we are a smaller team, and we always will be because there's absolutely no way that that amount of money, the gross figure which we're allowed, there's no way it's going to finance an extra counsel. We are always, on those figures, with the need for people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the need for a first class case manager, and because of Ms. Loukas being a Greek Australian - that's a complimentary term, especially this month - and me being English, which is a neutral term, no doubt, but it's simply a fact, we need Ms. Cmeric and we need Ms. Cmeric's Serbian desperately. She is a tremendous asset to the team. But we will never have the ability, on these arrangements, to put in an extra counsel. We are doing what we can, and it costs us money as well, but we plugged in a very high quality team of assistants and interns but that is as much as we will ever be able to do. And with Ms. Loukas and me as the -- having to do between us all the witnesses, all the burden, it is always going to be necessary throughout this trial for there to be careful assessment of positions so that the equality between us and the Prosecution can be achieved by ensuring that because we are a smaller team we're not faced with an inappropriate burden which does then produce a disparity. So the -- Your Honours have, and we appreciate that very much, Your Honours have given us a very full opportunity this afternoon of elaborating these points, and we are grateful for that because we feel that it has been necessary to do so. We -- we would wish to draw to Your Honours' attention particularly one matter and perhaps I should just explain by way of introduction because it's something to be just slightly cautious about the way I present it to Your Honours. I -- Your Honour may or may not know this, I'm a member of the advisory panel of this institution, and we had a meeting last week. There are various documents. They're not only available to members of the advisory panel, as it happens, but I was able to see them in that context. They're also available to members of the Association of Defence Counsel but they're publicly available. There are negotiations under way between the Registry and the Association of Defence Counsel in relation to various aspects of payment schemes. Those are in negotiation. There is a lot of confidential material. I'm not proposing to lay that confidential material before the Tribunal this afternoon, but I want to make it clear that is only because some of it is confidential and not because we have any wish to withhold any of that material or to take anything out of context, but I have spoken to the Registry in the course of the morning because I indicated to them particular points that I did wish to bring to the attention of this Trial Chamber out of that material, as a courtesy, but also in case they did have any objection and we were able to reach an understanding about what I might fairly tell the Trial Chamber. And what I can tell you, Your Honour, is that pre-trial preparation being split, for the purposes of those discussions, into phases 1, 2 and 3, but phase 1 being a very short phase, actually, the sort of introductory phase, phase 2 being preliminary motions and suchlike matters, and not being an enormous phase itself, so phase 3 then being really the substantial preparation, preserving the category of 1, 2 and 3 of cases, so that the top level, or the most demanding level, is a category 3 case in which this falls. Not very many cases do fall in category 3, but even when they do, this is actually -- this case is pretty high up the range within category 3, so it's certainly not simply an average category 3 case. If there were a category 4, this case would be in it. I assert that, but I assert it confidently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say a heavy category 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Heavy category 3" is absolutely apt for my purposes, Your Honour. I'm obliged. Now, for a category 3 case, simply as a single, undifferentiated category, the proposal is -- and there does seem to be a measure of agreement, as it happens, in relation to the matter. The proposal is that, as a guideline, preparation will involve nine months full time for lead counsel and five months full time co-counsel. Now, of course the Trial Chamber's not bound by that view. That's part of a payment scheme. On the other hand, it does, after all, reflect proposals. The Registry is not likely to make financial proposals which are out of line with -- well, they're not likely to overstate the amount of time needed to prepare a case. I'm not implying they would understate, but I'm simply making the fairly obvious assertion that, as husbanders of the budget as well, they're not likely to overstate it and wish to pay for much longer periods. So that the guidelines, nine months full time lead counsel, five months co-counsel, it's just -- it's a very valuable cross-check, Your Honour. We're not coming here and saying: That's what's under discussion. That's the answer. Give us that. And in fact, we're not asking for that anywhere, as it happens. But the disparity between that sort of assessment of an average category 3 case, if I can call that, because any category 3 case is far from average, in any serious sense of the matter, and what we have had. Even if you put together every week that is, if you like, theoretically -- or has theoretically been at our disposal, and for all sorts of reasons they haven't been, and even if you assume, if you like, just normal in all the essential aspects of the case, we have had nowhere near that. And that is a most valuable cross-check, but simply supportive of everything else we said. We don't rely on that. That's not the answer. That's not -- we finish there. Because it's not our starting point. It is not, in a sense, our finishing point. It's just -- we're nearly finished, I think. It's just a very useful cross-check. So even if we were to count every break we've had as a hundred per cent preparation time, which, for all sorts of reasons, as we've given them, is absolutely unreal, we come absolutely nowhere near. So where we do finish, and we nearly are there, Your Honour, is that the Defence don't deny that resources are relevant in the management of a case. Of course they are. And as it happens, both Ms. Loukas and I have experience in sitting as judges as well. So we do know a little bit about that from different perspectives. But we wouldn't want that remark to be quoted out of context, because where resources are limited, we accept that no defendant can expect more than the minimum needed for a fair trial. He might get it at times, but they're not entitled to it. They can't expect it. So the minimum needed for fair trial and fair presentation is the entitlement. And of course, a Defence team can expect to be put under heavy demands, as professionals, because that's what we like to think we are, and we technically certainly are. It shouldn't be to the point where it's unconscionable or in breach of any basis on which we join the case, but risks cannot be taken with a fair trial. If there's any doubt, you give the benefit to the defendant. Now, we live in the real world. The gravity of the charges and the potential sentence if convicted are highly material. It's common sense that while the principles are the same, courts don't agonise all that much if somebody is up on a careless driving charge. It's not the end of the world there. It's a fair trial, if there is a trial in relation to such a charge, is the principle. It is what's achieved. But of course it's a different exercise. It's of a totally different scale, or a minor assault. The courts have got to be careful, but they don't have to -- they don't have the heavy responsibility as any Trial Chamber has in relation to these sort of charges in this sort of case. There are competing pressures. We acknowledge that. There's the budget. There's always a budget. There's always a budget everywhere in the world, on everything. There's the UN budget. Heaven knows it's got its own problems. There's the Security Council. Heaven knows they've got their problems and worries too. Of course it's the responsibility of the President of this Tribunal to manage the entire institution, and it's -- of course it's the part of the important function of Your Honours to support the President and loyally to participate in the effective management of this institution. We know that out there in the real world - and it's in this building - is the completion strategy. We know that. All these things tie in together. And, well, to say that the budget is hard to control, everybody knows that as well. And it's not always successful, but there isn't always success. We know all that. But none of this can override essential rights. When we are not within the confines of this courtroom - because the public is out there and they're here in the gallery and they're out in the world outside - but when we are in this courtroom, those pressures are there, but Your Honours, as the Judges on any particular case, there comes a point where those pressures just have to be ignored. If they involve any significant risk to a fair defence, they have to be put on one side. And logically, and in practice, they are irrelevant to the assessment of the time needed. Once it is clear that time is necessary, not a luxury, once it's clear that time is necessary for a fair trial and a fair opportunity to present a defence, there are only two choices: the time is allowed or the charges are dropped. Those are the only two possible choices. So I -- and with an apology, Your Honour, I shouldn't have underestimated this problem for so long, and I shouldn't have brushed aside, as I sometimes did, some of the things that my own Defence team said. It's my job sometimes to brush things aside. Sometimes you get it right brushing things aside and sometimes you don't. And I should have brought all this very specifically to the Trial Chamber a long time ago, and I wish I had, but I have done today, and the Trial Chamber has to look at it now, in the circumstances now, and we do need this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution -- but perhaps we first have a -- we need a break anyhow, also for technical reasons, such as tapes. So therefore, I take the opportunity at least to put one question to you. When you are talking about the nine month and the five month, nine months for lead counsel, five months for co-counsel, would that stage of the proceedings include the preparation of a pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sure it would. I can double-check that, Your Honour but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But just for my --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's new information for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll double-check that over the break, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm 99 per cent sure it does, of course, and I've acknowledged that that task was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you mentioned two very important members of the -- of what constitutes a Defence team. At the same time, and I think rightly, you have drawn our attention also to the case manager. So would -- is there any standard for case management, involvement in that time as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour. May I -- I might be able to check this immediately, actually, and then that would be a help to Your Honours. But if not, then I -- perhaps I might do that over the -- over the break. I rather -- I rather promised the Registry that I wouldn't quote from this document. May I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's another matter. Then perhaps, if we have a break anyhow, perhaps you could be in touch with the Registrar and ask permission to give some quotes in private session. Well, then, it will only take one or two minutes, and then you could fully inform us. It's new information for us. We'd like to be as well informed as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed. Well, Your Honour, certainly that suggestion is very helpful. I also did -- it may not be necessary. I'll follow Your Honour's suggestion immediately. It was indicated to me that, of course, if the Trial Chamber felt at any time that it would like to see this material, then it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it could be -- yes. Well, perhaps you first seek permission to give the few quotes you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I half suspect that some of the people involved might even be watching and listening to what Your Honour is saying anyway, so the communication might be quite rapid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it could be, if everyone is watching on the screen. Then as far as these proceedings are concerned, I'd like to adjourn for 20 minutes. I'd then like to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to respond. Do you have any idea, Mr. Harmon, how much time that would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not more than 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not more than 15 minutes. So that means I would then like to give an additional opportunity to respond, to the extent wished, to the observations made by the Prosecution. So that altogether I take it would informing the Chamber hearing not more than 15 minutes, I take it that your response could also be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's bound to be pretty short, Your Honour, in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would take altogether approximately half an hour. Then I'd like to adjourn again so that the Judges can deliberate on the question whether we'd give a decision right away, even if that would be just an oral decision at this moment, which does not mean that such a decision would not be put on paper, and then it would be put on paper quite soon. But I also do understand that the Prosecution needs an answer very quickly on how we will proceed, because they're at this moment presenting their case. So therefore, for scheduling, I think we should give a decision as soon as possible, but of course we have to consider whether we can do it this afternoon or not, and therefore I'd like to ask the parties to remain available after this half hour when we are adjourning and to come back in Court as soon as we have made up our mind whether to decide this afternoon yes or no. We will then adjourn until five minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We apologise for a bit of a late start, but just as we are convinced that the Defence is using its time as efficiently as possible even if we don't see it, the parties are invited to believe that the Trial Chamber used its time as efficiently as possible, even for the additional ten minutes. Mr. Harmon, perhaps first we ask Mr. Stewart whether there is any additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke to the acting chief of OLAD. To be fair, they are a little reluctant to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One question I can answer, Your Honour, which is in relation to the question Your Honour asked me at the very end. The -- the case manager is not specifically identified as an item because the policy, I think, is to allow flexibility to lead counsel in how the team is constituted, so the -- what -- I don't think there's any mystery about this bit: Lump sum payments, which is the way it's done at the moment, after all, it's done on the basis that it requires one counsel, which would be lead counsel, and five support staff full time for nine months -- sorry, I'm reading the wrong -- I think I'm reading -- that's right. One counsel, five support staff and nine months, and then co-counsel to join for the last five months. So it's simply described as five support staff and it can be done anyway you like, but that's a very general term, and of course, well, it includes people whether they're here, there, or in Bosnia or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be investigators as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that when we're talking about month that we're talking about calendar month and not about -- you understand what I mean by a month? A month is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand what you mean. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- actually 22, 23 working days rather than 30 working days. Of course, I'm not saying that you're never working the weekend but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wasn't sure whether Your Honour was talking about lunar months for a moment, I wasn't quite sure whether they came into it. But Your Honour, what I understand to be meant by "months," actually, although it isn't spelled out, I think, there, is -- and I think this has been a feature of the similar arrangements for a long, long time is I think the figure taken has been 175 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Working hours, so I rather thought it as a rough guideline. I haven't really thought about it specifically, Your Honour, until a few minutes ago but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's approximately 22, 23 times eight hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's up to the individual how to spread it, Your Honour, but I think that's the position, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a better understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to indicate what rather reflected the discussion this morning, the suggestion was that if at some point the Trial Chamber felt it really did want to know more, then the options were private session, which was specifically acknowledged by OLAD, or also -- and/or a request by the Trial Chamber to OLAD to have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't make myself clear, Your Honour. The -- OLAD were not suggesting hand over the document to Your Honours and go into private session. What they were saying was, well, to quote bits from the document and explore some of these points, they would really wish it to be private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Your Honours wish to have the whole document, then they would appreciate the Trial Chamber making that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber got answers to the points that were unclear to it, and therefore, as far as the Chamber is concerned, there's no need to go into private session since we have no further questions on it and there's no specific wish to be provided with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did hand in a document because it really ties in very directly with the very questions Your Honour has just been asking in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for verification, then. Well, first of all, if you give this information, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber is, as such, inclined to believe you, unless you say there's really very relevant information on those in this document as well which would not -- would -- if -- if we would not have knowledge of that, it would prevent us from understanding what we wanted to know, and that is approximately what time and what resources are granted in this third pre-trial stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, as far as that's concerned, Your Honour, that topic is -- I appreciate what Your Honour has just said. As far as I'm concerned, it can be left there, we don't press any more. No. The other document that was tied in with this was -- and we would ask for this to be confidential, Your Honour, if that's the right way of dealing with it. We've given a schedule of the billable hours that the three of us here, myself, Ms. Loukas and Ms. Cmeric, did for August through to April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the time you have presented to the Registry as time used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would very much like to receive that as a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, should I comment on it now, or perhaps -- it's a very brief comment but there is a little bit of explanation. I can deal it easily after Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to deal with it in private session, being the document confidential or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not so -- I'm not so worried about that, Your Honour, no. I'd prefer that the entire document were not simply in the public domain, but the points I'm going to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document then is not in the public domain. That means that it's -- that it's submitted confidentially to the Trial Chamber. Then I think it has to get an exhibit number as well. Are you aware of what exhibit number should be attributed to it, Mr. Registrar? Let's deal with the number at a later stage. Even if it would not have immediately a number, it gets a number and there could be no confusion about the document. Could you please provide the copies of the documents to the Judges. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say you could briefly make some observations. Take it in a couple of minutes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour. The way -- what I'm saying, by definition I'm quite happy to say in open court. The normal allowance for preparation for the Defence counsel was 2.800 hours as far as the Registry was concerned. They allowed us 2.100 hours of pre-trial preparation on the footing that-- fairly rough and ready, but on the footing that 700 hours had effectively been saved for us by the work of Mr. Brashich, our predecessors. Actually, these figures total up -- then because the trial was started, in a sense, prematurely -- I think that is at least acknowledged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, 2.100 would be counsel hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Counsel hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Counsel hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would include you and Mrs. Loukas and would exclude Ms. Cmeric?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excluding Ms. Cmeric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- but included -- it actually also included legal consultant hours. So some of those hours went to Mr. Neskovic since we came on board, but not a significant number, Your Honour. This can -- for the purposes of this hearing, really, that can be disregarded. The -- the point is that the total -- we've had to estimate for March and April because I'm afraid we haven't found time to do the billing which -- for which a deadline comes up very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There are some notes indicating this. But the total then is 834 for me - that's right up to Easter - and 813 and some minutes -- say 814, if you round it up, for Ms. Loukas. So the reason I mention this, Your Honour, because it responds to Your Honour's observation about what's a month. If we take a month as 175 hours, which is, we'd suggest, that is a reasonable guideline, that's a full-time month, that seems -- that seems fair. The -- Your Honour can see the pattern.
