The -- in August, for example, with Ms. Loukas, in August she was here for that period in August, and we -- that's a period during which, for example, we spent a week with a lot of time with Mr. Krajisnik, some time with Mr. Brashich. As a matter of fact, at that point, bluntly, there was also a question of whether Ms. Loukas would be assigned, and lots of meetings with Mr. Krajisnik with the circumstances of the changeover were necessary. Quite a few were necessary before he was at all comfortable with me and then it's a question of appointment of co-counsel. So it wasn't so much work on the case there as convincing Mr. Krajisnik that we were the people who should represent him. The -- and then Your Honour can see that Ms. Loukas, in September, that's not much at all because she's still at work in Australia. The -- the big advantage, among her many other qualities, of course, of having Ms. Loukas involved, is she is full time and is available to be here in The Hague, much more than somebody who is having to jump backwards and forwards to London might be. So Your Honour can see the pattern. And also, with me, I simply observe, for example, Your Honour can see in December, it's quite obvious that in December that I -- I wasn't inclined to sit around and twiddle my thumbs for a period and just have a huge long rest. Although I can't and there's no reason why I should give Your Honour the details, of course I couldn't. Obviously, I must have been also engaged on -- on other things, which is unsurprising because I had to be, really, at many points. So that was just a fact. I am a full-time practising barrister who jumped into this case in -- in August, and frankly, anybody else they might have got in that category would have been in a similar position, unless, of course, they were pretty useless altogether and had nothing else to do. So that's the position, and Your Honour can see the pattern. And may I also point out, Your Honour, that in February we had of course started the trial, so during that month we spent many hours in court, but these are in addition to the hours in court. But of course by that time it's all getting tangled up with trial work as well. So a lot of what we're doing in February is actually not really pre-trial work at all but we're in trial. So it's -- these hours would in effect overstate. The last observation I'd make, Your Honour, and this is on the pre-trial brief, that the pre-trial brief has in fact -- the fact that it had been done by Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich, one shouldn't look at whatever hours they did or didn't put in. One way of starting it is, well, yes, it has saved us the task of doing that but what it's actually saved us is the task of writing out the pre-trial brief because it's left us with the task of doing the work. Because so far as the information and material is not there in the pre-trial brief handed over to us, and it largely isn't, frankly, because it doesn't tell you very much that you wouldn't be able to glean from the indictment and a couple of other documents, we've still got to do the work. It does save us the time of actually writing out the pre-trial brief, because once you've done the work, writing out these things is not the big task. I can write these things out in a day or two, or less sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean to say that repeating the word "no" very often or denying something doesn't take that much time, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's -- that's one point, Your Honour. But my other point was this: Because that didn't tell us very much, so as part of our pre-trial preparation we've got to do the work that would be required. Writing out more than "no" is not most of the work. The writing out is -- that's not the work. It's knowing what you're going to write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Making up your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just ask you, to see whether I followed you well. First of all, I think you said something about 813, 814 hours, something you were not quite sure about. Could you please repeat it because I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the addition of all the figures in the column under my initials. The addition of all the figures there is 834 and 40 minutes, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you just to follow my calculation and to comment on it where it seems to be incorrect, because of course we've only been provided with the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Appreciate that, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried to add all the time for two counsel, that is therefore Stewart, Loukas, up till the start of the trial, and I took that August up till January -- including January 2004, since the trial started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we've done that, Your Honour, so we can double check the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I come to approximately -- it's a rough calculation, but approximately 1.050 hours for the two counsel up to January. Is that a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that would -- well, yes, because we've actually calculated through to February, and I can see immediately just looking at the figures that Your Honour's figures are as close -- I'm sure they're absolutely accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had in mind approximately 1.045.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would then take you to the subsequent period, would you agree with me that if a trial starts normally, that part of the day is absorbed by activity at trial itself and then in court and some time remaining which is very often used for either preparing for the next day witness or the next week witness and some additional information and perhaps writing a motion or whatever. So it's additional work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is how life goes, Your Honour, we agree 100 per cent with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore for every day we're not sitting --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- more time is available because if the next day we are not sitting either, then of course you don't have to prepare for the witness of tomorrow and you're not spending any time in court. I calculated that -- well, let's say approximately up till this moment we have not been sitting for approximately 70 days where we could have been sitting. I'm not saying that -- that there are not several ways of using those days. Seventy days, two counsel, make 140 days. Let's just assume eight hours a day. That would make eight times 140, would make 1.120 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.045 and 1.120, taken together, is approximately 2.150, which is approximately the time, as I understand, attributed by the Registry for the third stage where 2.800 hours were reduced to 2.100 hours. Is that a correct calculation? Not whether or not it's fair to grant only 2.100 but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the arithmetic works, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it therefore be correct to say that the time you used up till the start of the trial in -- on the 3rd of February and the time that became available by not sitting - I'm not talking about negotiation, whatever, but just that time together - equals approximate 2.100 hours as was granted to you by the Registrar for the first stage of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the extraordinarily simplistic arithmetic works, yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether I'm simple or not is another matter but ---

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is not in the least bit simple, but complex highly intelligent people can produce very simplistic calculations, Your Honour, is what we're saying. And they are. When I get an opportunity, it might be better --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll get an opportunity to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, because I would like to make my assertion good on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd first like to hear from the Prosecution to respond to what has been said until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a unique motion. It is not one that I have seen nor had to respond to, and it's one that I should say the Prosecutor has always stated in this case that it's ready to proceed on any schedule provided by this Court, and I would like to reiterate that. We're prepared to continue with the trial on the schedule with the allotted number of hours and the allotted number of witnesses that the Court has indicated previously. This is an application by the Defence that's based on unique reasons given by the Defence for problems that they believe have impeded their ability to prepare completely for this trial and for which they believe impinge on Mr. Krajisnik's right to a fair trial. Many of those reasons we don't take issue with nor can we. The condition of the materials that were transmitted by the previous Defence team, the organisation of those materials to Mr. Stewart are factors that we offer no comment on and we accept without reservation the descriptions provided by Mr. Stewart. There are some matters in the submissions, both the written and oral submissions of Mr. Stewart, that I do think deserve some observations by the Prosecutor. Mr. Stewart came on this case on the 30th of July, 2003, and when we -- when he came on the case, and he says, and quite candidly, that he was unfamiliar other than as an educated person with facts dealing with the events in Yugoslavia, we helped or tried to assist Mr. Stewart when he came because we provided him on that day with a copy of the amended consolidated indictment, our pre-trial brief of the 2nd of May, 2002. We provided him with a list of witnesses pursuant to Rule 65 ter, a list of exhibits. We provided him with a revised exhibit list. We provided him with 92 bis material and yet another revised list of exhibits. So right away there was material that we attempted to provide to Mr. Stewart and his team that would have assisted Mr. Stewart in understanding this case. Additionally, there is an individual whose name I just heard, Goran Neskovic. Mr. Neskovic -- and if I'm wrong, Mr. Stewart can assist me and correct me on this, but if I'm wrong, Mr. Neskovic may still be associated with this case in some capacity. I'm speculating perhaps, and Mr. Stewart, if you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct. He is still officially a member of the Defence team. That's as much as I'm saying, but he is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Neskovic was initially lead counsel on this case for a period of three months. He was then co-counsel in this case for a number of months, and then he was a consultant. And I just refer Your Honours to a pleading that I do believe is a public pleading of July the 1st, 2002. It's the Registry comments, and it reflects that Mr. Neskovic at least billed approximately 4.300 hours to this institution for his work in the capacities of counsel and as a consultant. So Mr. Neskovic is somebody who has been a member of this team and who is familiar with this case. And indeed in a hearing that was before this Tribunal on the 13th of May 2003, and before Your Honour Judge Orie, Mr. Neskovic said, and I quote, and this is found at page 133 of the hearing of May the 13th, first of all, and I am quoting him: "I am very well acquainted with the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know the people," and as he goes on to say, "I have been working for Mr. Krajisnik for three years now." So in terms of understanding this case and developing a competent and complete understanding of this case, at least Mr. Neskovic was available for consultations and assisting the Defence. In addition, in terms of the opportunities to prepare, as a matter of public record, the Trial Chamber was accommodating. It did have a schedule that was -- the first part of this trial was, I think, 17 or 17 and a half days, followed by a recess, and we as members of the Prosecution team attempted to assist the Defence as well by identifying well in advance the names of the witnesses and the materials that the witnesses would be referring to to the Defence, and indeed sometimes we took our witnesses who we would call in particular order of proof out of schedule, out of sync in order to accommodate the Defence so they would have more time to prepare. I do think there is one matter that is raised in written the submissions of Mr. Stewart that I think deserves comment, and I do indeed want to comment on it. And it is found on page 7 of the submission in point 18. And I know it's not an issue, the size of the Prosecution team, however, I think it is worth mentioning where Mr. Stewart says that compared to the Prosecution team, six different counsel have conducted witness examinations. We do have a core Prosecution team. It consists of four lawyers; myself, Mr. Tieger, Mr. Hannis, and Ms. Karagiannakis, who will soon be leaving the Tribunal, so we will be down to three. In, I think it was May of -- I'll find the exact date for Your Honours, if I can. I don't have it at my disposal but it was in 2002, in a 65 ter conference with Judge May, I explicitly raised the issue of young lawyers participating in Tribunal proceedings in order to assist them in career development because it was my belief and it remains my belief that young lawyers are the future of this type of law and this type of work, and I raised the issue with Defence counsel then and with Judge May later, and I do believe possibly with this Chamber, because I was anxious to avoid any criticism of the optics of having more lawyers in court than the Defence. And in the hearing before -- it was Yvonne Featherstone in the 65 ter conference, I received an assurance from the Defence, that Defence team, that that would not be considered to be an issue. Now, I know it's not an issue, the size of the Prosecution team is not an issue in this case. Mr. Stewart says he has an adequately sized Defence team, but I wanted to bring that -- I wanted to comment on that particular aspect of the written submission. And I'd like to comment as well, just to make the record perfectly clear, that the -- and Mr. Stewart acknowledges in his written submission that Prosecution counsel - and the core counsel is what I'm referring to but also the junior lawyers - have additional responsibilities. It is not as though the Office of the Prosecutor lawyers are working exclusively and solely on this case. I will just briefly and very quickly identify, for example, at the same time I have been working on this case I was involved in the Deronjic case and I was involved in the Cesic case. We've been involved in the Ljubicic prosecution. I've been involved in other matters that I need not elaborate further. Mr. Tieger has been involved in the Mrdja case at the same time. Mr. Hannis has been involved in the Cesic case at the same time. My point is, so the record is perfectly clear, the Prosecution lawyers who are assigned to this case do indeed have additional responsibilities and fulsome responsibilities. Having said that, Your Honour, and having said that I do believe we are ready to proceed at any time on any schedule that Your Honours give us, I would like to point out two things that we do require, and Your Honour mentioned one of them. We do need to have a date certain at least for when the trial will start. We need to do that because we have motions outstanding. We would like to have -- make applications for the issuance of subpoenas and there could be no return on those subpoenas absent a firm court date. Second of all, there are a number of motions for which we await a decision -- decisions, and those motions have been suspended during the opportunity -- during the opportunity the Court gave the parties to try to resolve agreed upon facts. We are awaiting now -- it seems to me the landscape has changed, and we are awaiting a decision -- decisions from the Court that will help guide us in our further planning and presentation of the evidence. I specifically refer to 92 bis applications, decisions in Banja Luka, Prijedor, and Bosanska Krupa, as well as an outstanding decision on adjudicated facts. We have submitted virtually all of our 92 bis applications. We may be making some supplemental submissions in light of additional testimonies that have occurred since we made those submissions, but we had agreed earlier to have a schedule of responses given by the Defence. We're prepared, and we will as soon as we get a date and we formulate the next order of proof, we will be resubmitting to the Defence a schedule by which we think is reasonable for them to respond. In the final analysis, Your Honours, the submissions made by the Defence must stand on virtually the facts asserted in the motion. As I say, we will take a neutral position in this motion. We cannot contest many of the facts that have been submitted by the Defence, and with that, Your Honour, I have no further submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no questions for you, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Stewart, you are given the opportunity now to respond. But perhaps before doing so, you could perhaps include some of the -- some of the few questions I would have -- I would like to put to you just for my better understanding of the confidential document. Do I well understand that March and April, the figures appearing there are the approximate figures of time spent in addition to the trial work? That means preparation for trial and -- is that a correct understanding or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We weren't in trial, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I'm not quite following. In which months; March and April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: March and April. Well, in April we had some trial time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the April figures only go up to Easter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We finished on the 27th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: March is then -- well, let's say the figures then are the figures spent -- and do I then also understand that the number appearing for March, as far as you're concerned, is influenced by what you have written down as other matters you had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I -- I'll come back to that arithmetical point in a moment. Your Honour, may I just say in -- with reference to my last slightly irritable response, I see my own Defence team but I don't see myself as immune from this. We have worked beyond what -- I say "at least" in the motion. We have worked beyond what any Trial Chamber can reasonably expect. If you allow -- I take out that lump, for example, and I had to be engaged on something else, but I was working then as well, after all. But when we have been here day in, day out, we have worked beyond it. That's -- that's a simple fact. And we just ask some regard to be paid to that. We are professionals. We did come here expecting to work hard, but month in, month out, we must not be abused, with respect. And I will not allow my team to be abused. That is why I made it clear to Your Honour that I'm insisting that my team have a proper break over the imminent recess. I will not allow, with respect, I simply will not allow that recess to be absorbed by adding work for them when they must have that break. And I say no more about that, Your Honour, because it's the facts, really, that speak for themselves here, and I don't -- I don't wish to pursue that particular tone, but I am the leader of this Defence team, and I do have some strong feelings in that area, Your Honour. The -- so far as the observations made by Mr. Harmon are concerned, Mr. Neskovic -- actually, I had no idea whatever, I'm afraid, that Mr. Neskovic had billed 4.300 hours in this case, because most of his billing, after all, was during a period of which I was not concerned. As a matter of fact, I'm shocked, but never mind. That's ancient history, but as far as our preparation of the case is concerned. Mr. Neskovic is in Doboj. Mr. Neskovic doesn't speak English. I'm not in Doboj. I am -- I live in London when I'm not here, which I now am pretty much all the time. I don't speak Serbian. I'm afraid -- Mr. Harmon was not intending to be in the least bit unhelpful. Mr. Harmon is giving the Court the facts. I can't possibly quarrel with that. But the facts are that whatever Mr. Neskovic has been doing, he doesn't speak English, I don't speak Serbian, he's in Doboj, I'm not in Doboj, the opportunity -- we have had some input from Mr. Neskovic, yes, occasionally had a briefing, but it has to come, effectively, in writing from Mr. Neskovic through Ms. Cmeric to me. It's not the most effective way of transmitting information from one brain to another. It might be more effective for the Brashich matter, but it's marginal, Your Honour. So that really is no significant benefit, and that's not disparaging Mr. Neskovic who has a Serbian speaking lawyer in Doboj, and I'm not criticising him for that, it's just that he can be of limited help to us. Mr. Harmon is right; I make not the slightest criticism of the size of the Prosecution team. I'm not blaming Mr. Harmon for not jettisoning bits of his team, and I did positively endorse his suggestion in relation to bringing other people on the team and I make absolutely no criticism of it at all. I simply observe that, again, I don't require the Prosecution team to jettison the knowledge they have in their brain but these three very experienced lawyers who constitute the core Prosecution team have absorbed years and years of knowledge of the background in relation to all these matters from their involvement in other cases, knowledge which we do not have and have had to catch up on. And it's quite true that Mr. Harmon did supply me with much of that material. The consolidated indictment is available on the website anyway, but thank you, I appreciated having the hard copies. The -- but that's not what I was talking about anyway. There's a lot of extra work to actually understand what's going on. The -- Your Honour also will be aware from being involved in these matters that there's a tremendous lot of time for which you don't get to charge at all. When I spent four days Belgrade-Bosnia, Bosnia-Belgrade, I was only actually able to charge 12 hours for being away four days, from early in the morning to getting back late on Friday night. And 12 hours, 12 chargeable hours because you can't charge when you're driving from Pale to Banja Luka or whatever. You can't do it. And Your Honour knows the way that works. So -- and when I'm, in the early days, travelling backwards and forwards from London, there are an awful lot of hours devoted to this case which don't appear there. But -- so that's just extra strain on the team if it has to do that, but the actual arithmetic when one adds it up here, once we get into the trial stage -- the problem in February is that when we look, for example, at those more or less a hundred hours each for Ms. Loukas and myself, so we were doing -- we had 17 and a bit days in court, so we had about 85 hours or something like that in court, so we got 185 hours, plus I've got about a day or so a month of all this admin. and billing and invoicing and so on. Every day, of course, I have lots of other stuff for which I can't charge, it's not in court, so actually it's a lot more, as a physical exercise, it's a lot more than that full time working month, there is no question about that. But those hours in February, a lot of them are not then pre-trial preparation at all. They're -- and I hope the Registry are not going to start chopping great chunks off our bill because I make that comment, and that would rather peeve me, I must say, but the simple fact is that it's not, that once you're in trial, you're working on the trial. The day, as Your Honour described it, is exactly right, but the month in February, which was intensely high pressure for us -- and that was acknowledged by Mr. Harhoff expressly in e-mails, it's certainly acknowledged by the Prosecution and Your Honours. There's no pre-trial preparation worth speaking of there, so you can please chop out those hours for a start. When we -- when we get into March, the fact that on a calculation of days out of court so many hours are available, well, for reasons I've given to Your Honour they weren't available, and neither Mr. Krajisnik nor I can or should be penalised for the fact that in the circumstances in which I came into this case I was not available all the time every month every day to do this case. I've made myself available when I can. Once we get into March and April, well, in a way, yes, sort of pre-trial preparation in the sense that I'm -- a lot of time spent preparing for Mr. Treanor, but once you've started the trial you're then wrapped up in all sorts of things which are to do with the trial and not pre-trial preparations. So the -- the arithmetic -- that's why, with respect, Your Honour, I say it's simplistic, the arithmetic simply doesn't work. And what I'm beginning to get concerned about here, Your Honour, is that I've given Your Honour these figures as a cross-check, and myself, I didn't suggest they were any more than some sort of broad cross-check, and immediately, with respect, Your Honour is coming back at me, doing the calculations, doing the arithmetic, in the way we've become so familiar with in this case, to demonstrate something which is simply a fact, which is we have not had enough time to prepare this case. We are overwhelmed with material for this case, we simply must have time to do it. It was only a cross-check. It is a fact, and you could put a mainframe computer on it for years, and whatever result the mainframe computer produces it is a simple fact that we need this time to prepare. And I do believe that arithmetic aside, I do believe that I have explained it all sorts of ways, the features of this case. The arithmetic doesn't alter the piles of documents still to be examined, still to be read. It doesn't read them. And presenting documents to us doesn't read them for us, and Mr. Neskovic out in Doboj doesn't read this stuff for us. We have to do this. And in fact, Your Honour, if one makes an actual practical adjustment of the figures, and if you allow for the fact that the 92 bis stuff, which is not pre-trial preparation really, even if it can come up at pre-trial stage, it really isn't, the way the 92 bis stuff overwhelmed the two other members of my team here during that period was absolutely obvious to me. It's basically what they did. Ms. Loukas is pretty much known as Ms. 92 bis. That's what she did for all that time. And with Ms. Cmeric, sorting out all the stuff so we could work on it, most of the time. And then in the -- in the later stages, it has been a valiant attempt, I do appreciate that, Your Honour, to try to work around -- you know that, Your Honour, we did refuse to elect between those two options given to us some weeks ago, so we've never quite seen eye-to-eye on this, with respect, but there's at least been an attempt. But that on-off, on-off way of working has never really given us the opportunity to get on top of this. It's not just the days out of court. Whenever we finished a session of a couple of weeks' of evidence, there are days of catching up then. Even after a couple of weeks, there's at least two or three days of just sweeping up and catching up and sorting it out, and then if you're going to be back in court to do more evidence, then you've got days of getting ready for that. And it's a lot of days. The witnesses that have been dealt with, they're not lightweight witnesses, as Your Honour will appreciate, many of them. Quite an enormous amount of work. So the idea that this arithmetic can be done in such a way that it actually produces for us anything remotely like that, always in bearing in mind also, Your Honour, that inherent in all these schemes is the ability to -- to provide more funds. We're not asking for more funds, we're not saying that, but simply reminding Your Honour that those simple cross-check figures of nine months and five months and so on, those are for a category 3 case. And Your Honour rather accepted the proposition this is a heavy category 3 case, and once it becomes -- there simply isn't another category beyond 3. That's the thing; if there were, we'd be in it, but there isn't. Category 3 is, if you like, it's a category that's going to range from heavy cases to absolutely massive cases, and this is a massive case. I don't believe there is anything else I can say, Your Honour, except for the tiny point that I think 175 hours a month really works out to more of a 7-hour day rather than an 8-hour day, but that's a rather lame note to finish on, that's because we don't -- we use the arithmetic as a convenient cross-check, but all the circumstances of this case, as we've laid them out, just demonstrate, as we believe we've demonstrated, that we must have a fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik by having more time.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

Mr. Harmon, if a decision would be given today, when would be the earliest opportunity to hear evidence in the Prosecution's case? Would that be -- would -- it's now Friday. Would be Monday in one week enough? So that's, let's say, another ten days from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has preferred to take a little bit more time and give its decision orally at this moment. I will give the reasons for the decision to the extent possible. That means that it might not be complete. It might not be in every single word the reasons that will later on appear in a written decision, so the written decision is authoritative but leaving you without any idea of the reasons at all is not what the Chamber considered appropriate to do. This is then the decision on the Defence motion for adjournment. Defence counsel has relied on the fair trial guarantee as embodied in Article 21 of the Statute and asked for additional time for preparation of its Defence. As the Defence puts it, an opportunity to test every aspect of the Prosecution's case and to present the accused's defence is an essential element of a fair hearing. In paragraph 6 of its motion the Defence elaborates on sections 4 B, D, E of Article 21 of the Statute. Since the Defence does not claim that no opportunity has been given to it until now to examine Prosecution witnesses, and since the trial has not yet reached the stage when Defence is required to present its witness list and when decisions are taken on the number of witnesses that may be called or on the time available to the Defence to present its witnesses, the emphasis in the motion is on the right of the accused, assisted in this respect by counsel, to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of the defence. The essential issue, therefore, as rightly has been pointed out in paragraph 7 of the motion, is whether the time and facilities, and especially the time, given to the Defence are adequate. Time, together with other resources, is a vital factor when preparing a defence. The other resources will turn out to be without effect if no time is available to use them. The question of access to financial resources has been thoroughly litigated in this case, leaving only time as the main issue. What might be considered adequate time for the preparation of the defence? The case law of the international bodies, such as the European Court on Human Rights and the UN Committee on Human Rights is not of great guidance when it comes to making decisions on the specifics of this case. In general, however, the circumstances and the complexity of the case are mentioned as critical factors. The past and the present factual circumstances relating to the preparation of the Defence case does not seem to be in dispute. It is understood that the current Defence team took over from the former team with considerable difficulties. The Chamber is aware of only two members of the current team who have served on the former team, even if not throughout, the two of them. The communication with the accused, who is in detention, takes time and so does the travel of members of the team to the former Yugoslavia. The emphasis put by the Defence on the complexity of the case is therefore of special relevance, both as it relates to the factual allegations, namely the alleged crimes in a large number of municipalities involving a large number of actors and victims, and as it relates to questions of law. For example, it transpires from the indictment and from related documents that the legal responsibility charged encompasses joint criminal enterprise and the other aspects of Article 7.1 responsibility as well as command responsibility under Article 7.3. The Defence in that motion mainly concentrate on the extensive allegations of fact and the context as illustrated by the large amount of material involved in this case. The complexity of the cases before the Tribunal is obvious, especially in the category of so-called leadership cases. The essential aspects of the Prosecution's case seem to be fairly reflected by the Defence in paragraph 12 of its motion. The question, therefore, is what does adequate time mean in the context of this type of a case. A case in which the number of events and the structure of power and responsibility underlying the criminal charges cover a large territory, a long period of time, and many victims cannot possibly be dealt with as a whole at the same level of detail as a case of a different scale. This justifies limitations -- limitations in case presentation by the parties and it requires parties to find a balance between aspects to which greater or lesser attention will be given in the presentation of their cases -- of their cases. Within these limits, the full exploration of the historical context of the armed conflict necessarily competes, for example, for time with the need to verify or introduce details on the so-called crime base evidence or with the need to acquire a detailed understanding of the interactions in the various environments in which the accused is said to have operated. Having established that the -- that mastery of a case is a relative concept, as it also is in domestic trials of a complex nature, the Chamber has to determine whether the time granted in this case to the Defence for preparation has reasonably allowed it and will reasonably allow it to develop a competent defence while being aware, of course, that one always wishes to do better and always wishes to have more time in which to do so. Certainly it would be unacceptable if the time granted to Defence would fall below the minimum necessary to make the trial fair to the accused. Having taken into account the complexity of the case as outlined above, the late start of the present Defence team and the difficulties it faced and still faces, the chronology presented by the Defence including facts and circumstances beyond and within the control of the accused and the Defence team, the size of the Defence team and the contribution to the Defence the accused could provide, the time spent in court since the start of the trial, the time already granted to the Defence in the course of the trial as well as before the trial began, time granted to prepare, the general practice in this Tribunal, as in existence at this moment, to grant 2.800 counsel hours for the whole of the pre-trial stage in level 3 cases, the information provided by the Defence on the working hours reported to the Registry, and the performance of the highly qualified and competent Defence team until today, and having also considered all the submissions of the Defence and all their details, the Defence has not convinced the Chamber that either the schedule followed to this day or the envisaged schedule for the near future, which I shall outline in a moment and which includes further allowances for preparation, has violated or will violate the accused's right to adequate time for preparation of his Defence or that it has been or will be prejudicial to the fairness of the trial. The Trial Chamber will continue to closely monitor the issue as the trial continues. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber denies the motion and orders the trial to continue in accordance with the following schedule covering the period up until the 1st of November, 2004. The schedule is that in July, we will sit on the 26th, the 27th, the 28th, with some reservations which I will explain, and on the 29th and the 30th of July. I immediately give the explanation for this specific week. The last week of July the Plenary takes place, Plenary meeting of the Judges. That's the reason why we'll try to start, if courtrooms are available, in the morning hours, if possible including the 28th of July. On the other hand, we will try to sit on the 29th in the afternoon. So there is some reservation because the Judges have some duties in respect of attendance of the Plenary meeting. On the other hand, we'll try, to the extent possible, to sit on the 30th in the morning. We will then not sit in the week of the 23rd of August. So we will have a later start, that is, we'll sit starting the 30th of August up till the 3rd of September. That's one week. We'll sit on the 6th and the 7th of September. We will then resume on the -- let me check that I do not make any mistake. We will then resume on the 20th of September, and we'll continue sitting on from then the whole month of October. The schedule I have just read out results in 18 non-consecutive out-of-court days for further preparation instead of the 40 consecutive days the Defence has requested. The written decision will follow soon. This is the decision. Is there any other issue to be raised at this moment?
